title: Feature Construction and Feature Splitting
abstract:
The branch of feature engineering that no library can do for you. Feature
construction derives a new column from existing ones using intuition and domain
knowledge; feature splitting breaks one column into several. This document covers
the six construction patterns that account for most real gains — ratios,
differences, aggregates, interactions, group-relative values and splits —
worked through the Titanic family_size and title examples, with
the mathematics of why a ratio can succeed where neither raw column can, the
automated alternatives, and the leakage rules that group-relative features must
respect.

From the notes

Derive a new column with the help of other columns.
It might increase the model's performance.

 columns.

blocks.t: Why this is the highest-leverage step in the pipeline

Recall the Bayes-error argument (Topics 05, 12): no algorithm can extract
information that is not present in $X$. Every other technique in Part II
reshapes the information you already have — scaling, encoding,
imputation, outlier treatment. Feature construction is the only step that
adds information, by encoding a relationship a human knows about and the
data does not state explicitly.

That is why it is also the only step a library cannot automate: it requires
knowing what the columns mean.
The Patterns

blocks.cap:
Six patterns that account for the large majority of useful constructed
 features. When you are stuck, work through them in order against your column
 list.

blocks.t: Ratio

The single most productive pattern. A ratio makes two quantities comparable
across rows of different scale.

rows: Medicine cares about the ratio, not either number
Comparable across cities in a way raw price is not
Implied speed — 900 km/h between two card swipes is fraud

blocks.t: Why a linear model cannot construct a ratio for itself

A linear model fits $\hat y = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$. There is no choice of
$\beta_1,\beta_2$ that equals $x_1/x_2$, because a ratio is not in the model's
hypothesis space. The same holds for products and for any non-linear combination.

A tree can approximate a ratio by partitioning the plane into rectangles,
but the boundary $x_1/x_2 = c$ is a straight line through the origin — a
diagonal, which axis-aligned splits can only approach as a staircase, needing many
splits and many data points. Constructing the ratio gives the model in one column
what it would otherwise spend enormous capacity approximating.
Difference

Elapsed time is the most valuable instance and was covered in Topic 22:
days_since_signup generalises where signup_date does not. Others:
profit = revenue - cost, age_at_event = event_date - birth_date,
score_change = score_now - score_last_month.
Aggregate — the Titanic example
The notes' example, made concrete

Titanic has sibsp (siblings and spouses aboard) and parch (parents
and children aboard). Neither separates survivors well. But
family_size = sibsp + parch + 1

does, because survival was non-monotone in family size: solo travellers fared
badly, small families (2–4) fared well, and large families fared badly again —
they could not stay together.

blocks.cap:
Left: the two raw columns give no clean boundary. Middle: the
 constructed sum separates the classes with two thresholds. Right: the measured
 effect on cross-validated AUC, and the further gain from encoding the
 non-monotone shape as a binary is_small_family.

blocks.t: Notice the second step

family_size helps, but a linear model still fits a single slope across it
and cannot express "2–4 is good, everything else is bad". Adding
is_small_family = (2 <= family_size <= 4) encodes the shape directly.
This is feature construction and binning (Topic 20) working together, and the
combination is where most of the gain lives.
Interaction

Products: area = length $\times$ width,
revenue = price $\times$ quantity. Also indicator interactions —
is_weekend $\times$ is_promo captures an effect present only when
both hold. PolynomialFeatures generates all pairwise products
automatically, at the cost of $O(p^2)$ new columns.
Group-relative

Normalising a value against its own group is one of the strongest patterns in
practice: spend / user_mean_spend, or the $z$-score of a transaction
within a merchant category. It converts an absolute quantity into "unusual for
this entity", which is what most anomaly and personalisation problems actually
care about.
Group-relative features leak by construction

The group mean is computed from the data, which includes the row you are
encoding — and, if computed on the full dataset, includes the validation rows'
labels indirectly. Two rules:

items:
Compute group statistics on the training set only, and store them
 for use at serving time.

For a temporal problem, compute them using only data before the
 prediction timestamp — an expanding or rolling window, shifted by one
 period (Topic 22).

blocks.t: Feature Splitting
From the notes
Split the "Mr Ankit" column into 2 columns.

blocks.cap:
A name is not one signal, it is three. The title encodes age band, sex
 and marital status simultaneously — and on the Titanic, "Master" identifies
 a boy under about 13, which no other column states.

blocks.t:
This is the same operation as Case 1 in Topic 21 (mixed variables), applied
deliberately rather than defensively. Common splits:

rows: title, first name, surname (surname enables family grouping)
local part, domain (a free-mail domain is a signal in fraud)

blocks.t: Automated Alternatives, and Their Limits

head: Approach
What it does
Limit
rows: All products and powers up to degree $d$
$O(p^d)$ columns; no ratios; no domain meaning
Generates thousands of features, most useless; needs a relational schema
Expensive; prone to overfitting; results are hard to justify
Cannot represent ratios compactly; needs data to learn what you already know

blocks.t: Why automation does not replace this step

An automated system can generate $x_1/x_2$ among ten thousand other candidates.
It cannot tell you that $\text{distance}/\text{time}$ is implied speed and
that 900 km/h is physically impossible for a human — which is the fact that
makes the feature work. The generator produces candidates; domain knowledge
produces the right candidate, and does so without the multiple-testing
burden that comes with searching ten thousand of them.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name":     rng.choice(["Mr. Ankit Sharma", "Mrs. Priya Rao",
                            "Miss. Anita Das", "Master. Arjun Rao"], n),
    "sibsp":    rng.integers(0, 5, n),
    "parch":    rng.integers(0, 4, n),
    "fare":     rng.lognormal(3.2, .7, n),
    "weight":   rng.normal(70, 12, n),
    "height_m": rng.normal(1.70, .09, n),
    "user_id":  rng.integers(0, 200, n),
    "amount":   rng.lognormal(3.0, .8, n),
})

# =====================================================================
# 1. RATIO -- a linear model CANNOT construct this for itself
# =====================================================================
df["bmi"] = df.weight / df.height_m ** 2
y_health = (df.bmi > 25).astype(int)          # the truth depends ONLY on the ratio

raw = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                      df[["weight", "height_m"]], y_health, cv=5,
                      scoring="roc_auc").mean()
built = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                        df[["bmi"]], y_health, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"raw weight+height auc {raw:.4f}   constructed BMI auc {built:.4f}")

# Even a random forest struggles, because the boundary is a CURVE:
rf_raw = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
                         df[["weight", "height_m"]], y_health, cv=5,
                         scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"forest on raw columns auc {rf_raw:.4f} -- it approximates with a staircase")

# =====================================================================
# 2. AGGREGATE -- the Titanic family_size example
# =====================================================================
df["family_size"] = df.sibsp + df.parch + 1        # +1 for the passenger
# survival is NON-MONOTONE in family size
p = np.where((df.family_size >= 2) & (df.family_size <= 4), .70, .25)
y_surv = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)

print("\nsurvival rate by family size:")
print(df.assign(y=y_surv).groupby("family_size").y.agg(["mean", "size"]).round(3))

for label, cols in [("raw sibsp+parch", ["sibsp", "parch"]),
                    ("+ family_size",   ["sibsp", "parch", "family_size"])]:
    s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), df[cols], y_surv,
                        cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
    print(f"{label:18s} auc {s:.4f}")

# The non-monotone shape needs one more step (feature construction + binning):
df["is_alone"]         = (df.family_size == 1).astype(int)
df["is_small_family"]  = df.family_size.between(2, 4).astype(int)
df["is_large_family"]  = (df.family_size > 4).astype(int)
s = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                    df[["is_alone", "is_small_family", "is_large_family"]],
                    y_surv, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean()
print(f"{'+ shape encoded':18s} auc {s:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. FEATURE SPLITTING -- "Mr Ankit" into several columns
# =====================================================================
parts = df.name.str.extract(r"^(?P<title>[A-Za-z]+)\.\s+"
                            r"(?P<first>[A-Za-z]+)\s+(?P<last>[A-Za-z]+)$")
df = pd.concat([df, parts], axis=1)
print("\n", df[["name", "title", "first", "last"]].drop_duplicates().to_string(index=False))

# The title encodes SEX, AGE BAND and MARITAL STATUS at once:
title_meaning = {"Mr": "adult male", "Mrs": "married adult female",
                 "Miss": "unmarried female", "Master": "boy under ~13"}
print("\n", title_meaning)
# On the Titanic "Master" is the ONLY column identifying young boys -- and
# age is missing for 20% of passengers, so this recovers it for free.

# Surname enables family grouping -- a genuinely relational feature:
df["surname_group_size"] = df.groupby("last")["last"].transform("size")

# =====================================================================
# 4. GROUP-RELATIVE -- "unusual FOR THIS USER"
# =====================================================================
# WRONG: computed on all the data, including validation rows
df["amount_vs_user_LEAKY"] = df.amount / df.groupby("user_id").amount.transform("mean")

# RIGHT: statistics learned on TRAIN and stored for serving
class GroupRelative(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """x / group_mean(x), with the group means LEARNED from training data."""
    def __init__(self, group_col, value_col):
        self.group_col, self.value_col = group_col, value_col

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        self.means_ = X.groupby(self.group_col)[self.value_col].mean()
        self.global_ = X[self.value_col].mean()      # fallback for unseen groups
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        g = X[self.group_col].map(self.means_).fillna(self.global_)
        return (X[self.value_col] / g).to_frame("ratio_to_group")

tr, te = train_test_split(df, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
gr = GroupRelative("user_id", "amount").fit(tr)
print("\ntrain ratios:", gr.transform(tr).head(3).values.ravel().round(3))
print("test  ratios:", gr.transform(te).head(3).values.ravel().round(3))
print("unseen user falls back to the global mean:",
      gr.transform(pd.DataFrame([{"user_id": 9999, "amount": 50.0}])).values.round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE FRAUD EXAMPLE -- physics as a feature
# =====================================================================
txn = pd.DataFrame({
    "user":  [1, 1, 1, 2, 2],
    "ts":    pd.to_datetime(["2026-03-01 10:00", "2026-03-01 10:06",
                             "2026-03-01 14:00", "2026-03-01 09:00",
                             "2026-03-01 11:30"]),
    "lat":   [19.07, 28.61, 19.07, 12.97, 13.08],
    "lon":   [72.87, 77.20, 72.87, 77.59, 80.27],
})
txn = txn.sort_values(["user", "ts"])
txn["dt_hours"] = txn.groupby("user").ts.diff().dt.total_seconds() / 3600
# crude great-circle distance in km
dlat = txn.groupby("user").lat.diff(); dlon = txn.groupby("user").lon.diff()
txn["dist_km"] = np.sqrt((dlat*111)**2 + (dlon*111*np.cos(np.radians(txn.lat)))**2)
txn["implied_kmh"] = txn.dist_km / txn.dt_hours.replace(0, np.nan)
txn["impossible"] = txn.implied_kmh > 900          # faster than a jet
print("\n", txn[["user", "ts", "dist_km", "dt_hours", "implied_kmh", "impossible"]]
        .round(1).to_string(index=False))
# NEITHER raw column says anything. The ratio says "this cannot have happened."

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE AUTOMATED ALTERNATIVE, AND ITS COST
# =====================================================================
base = df[["weight", "height_m", "fare", "sibsp", "parch"]]
poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False).fit(base)
print(f"\nPolynomialFeatures: {base.shape[1]} columns -> "
      f"{len(poly.get_feature_names_out())} columns")
print("but it generates PRODUCTS, never RATIOS:",
      [c for c in poly.get_feature_names_out() if "/" in c] or "none")
# BMI = weight / height^2 is simply not in the space it searches.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE WHOLE THING AS A PIPELINE-SAFE TRANSFORMER
# =====================================================================
class FeatureConstructor(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Domain features. Stateless here, so fit() has nothing to learn."""
    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        X = X.copy()
        X["bmi"]             = X.weight / X.height_m ** 2
        X["family_size"]     = X.sibsp + X.parch + 1
        X["is_alone"]        = (X.family_size == 1).astype(int)
        X["is_small_family"] = X.family_size.between(2, 4).astype(int)
        X["fare_per_person"] = X.fare / X.family_size
        X["title"]           = X.name.str.extract(r"^([A-Za-z]+)\.")[0]
        return X.drop(columns=["name"])

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.array(["sibsp", "parch", "fare", "weight", "height_m",
                         "user_id", "amount", "bmi", "family_size", "is_alone",
                         "is_small_family", "fare_per_person", "title"])

cols = ["name", "sibsp", "parch", "fare", "weight", "height_m", "user_id", "amount"]
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("construct", FeatureConstructor()),
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["title"]),
        ("num", StandardScaler(), ["bmi", "family_size", "fare_per_person",
                                   "is_alone", "is_small_family", "fare"]),
    ], remainder="drop")),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
print("\nfull pipeline auc:",
      cross_val_score(pipe, df[cols], y_surv, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))
# Construction lives INSIDE the pipeline, so production applies the identical
# derivations -- no chance of computing family_size differently at serve time.
Summary
Everything on one page

 columns. It might increase the model's performance.

Feature splitting breaks one column into several —
 split "Mr Ankit" into title and name.

It is the only step in Part II that adds information rather than
 reshaping it, which is why it has the highest ceiling and cannot be
 automated away.

Six patterns: ratio, difference, aggregate, interaction,
 group-relative, split.

A linear model cannot construct a ratio — it is outside the
 hypothesis space. A tree can only approximate one with a staircase of
 axis-aligned splits.

The Titanic example: family_size = sibsp + parch + 1. The
 relationship is non-monotone, so encode the shape as well
 (is_alone, is_small_family).

Splitting a name yields title, which encodes sex, age band and
 marital status simultaneously.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Give an example of a constructed feature that beat the raw columns.

BMI. Neither weight nor height predicts obesity well on its own — a heavy person
may simply be tall. The ratio $\text{weight}/\text{height}^2$ is what medicine
actually uses, and a linear model cannot form it because a ratio is not in its
hypothesis space.
Q. Can't a gradient-boosted tree just learn the interaction itself?

Only approximately, and expensively. A ratio boundary $x_1/x_2 = c$ is a diagonal
line, which axis-aligned splits approximate as a staircase — many splits, and
many data points to justify each one. Handing the model the ratio directly costs
one column.

Q. Why is family_size better than sibsp and parch
separately?

Because survival depends on the total, and the dependence is non-monotone: solo
travellers and large families both fared badly, small families well. Neither raw
column shows that. Adding a binary is_small_family on top encodes the
shape a linear model otherwise cannot express.
Q. What does splitting a passenger name give you?

The title — Mr, Mrs, Miss, Master — which encodes sex, marital status and age
band at once. On the Titanic, "Master" identifies boys under about thirteen,
which is genuinely useful when age is missing for a fifth of the passengers.
The surname additionally enables family grouping.
Q. How do group-relative features leak, and how do you prevent it?

The group mean is computed from data that includes the row being encoded, and, if
computed on the full dataset, indirectly from validation rows. Compute group
statistics on the training set only, store them for serving with a global-mean
fallback for unseen groups, and for temporal problems use a window that ends
strictly before the prediction timestamp.
Q. Why not just use PolynomialFeatures and let the model choose?

It generates products and powers, never ratios, so it misses the most productive
pattern. It also produces $O(p^2)$ columns, most of them meaningless, which costs
compute and invites overfitting through multiple testing. Domain knowledge
produces the right candidate without searching thousands of wrong ones.
